notes.meaning: The heavenly guide leads Ezekiel out of the porch and into the Holy Place, the main room of the temple. He measures the doorposts on both sides of the entrance, and each one is six cubits thick. Together, these two posts equal twelve cubits, matching the entire width of the tent of worship that Moses built.

differ.view: These detailed measurements prove that an actual, physical temple will be built in Jerusalem during the end times.
The vision uses architectural pictures from Ezekiel's day to symbolize the spiritual perfection and security of Christ's church.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The description pointed in part toward the post-exilic temple, but its true fulfillment is found mystically in the Church of Christ.

notes.meaning: The doorway into the Holy Place is ten cubits wide, with side walls of five cubits flanking the opening. Inside, the room is forty cubits long and twenty cubits wide. These interior dimensions match the Holy Place of Solomon's temple, showing continuity in God's holy dwelling place.

The guide walks into the innermost room, but Ezekiel stays outside because priestly law forbade ordinary priests from entering the inner sanctuary. The guide measures the pillars of this inner entrance to be two cubits thick. The entrance itself is six cubits wide, framed by walls measuring seven cubits across.

The guide measures the inner room to be twenty cubits long and twenty cubits wide, forming a perfect square. He then tells Ezekiel that this space is the Most Holy Place, where the glory of God dwelled in earlier days. The perfect square shape reflects completeness, stability, and holy order.

The guide next measures the outer wall of the main temple structure, finding it to be six cubits thick. Built against the outside of this wall were side rooms that were four cubits wide. These side rooms surrounded the north, west, and south sides of the building to store sacred items and priestly garments.

The side rooms rose in three stories of thirty rooms each, making ninety rooms in total. The support beams rested on narrow ledges formed by steps in the temple wall rather than being cut into the holy walls themselves. Because the main wall stepped back and became narrower as it went up, the side rooms grew wider on each higher floor, reached by winding stairs.

differ.view: The side rooms widening as they ascend represent the church growing larger and more glorious as it draws closer to heaven.

notes.meaning: Ezekiel notices that the entire temple building sits upon a raised platform. This raised foundation for the side rooms is a full measuring rod high, which equals six long cubits. This platform elevated the sacred house above the surrounding courtyards.

The outer wall enclosing the side rooms was five cubits thick, and an open walkway ran outside them. A clear space of twenty cubits separated these side structures from the outer chambers around the court. The side rooms opened out toward this open area, with one entrance facing north and another facing south.

A separate building stood on the west side of the temple complex facing the courtyard. It was seventy cubits wide and ninety cubits long, enclosed by walls five cubits thick. While its exact function is not directly stated, it stood behind the sanctuary in a distinct yard.

The guide measures the full length of the temple structure, and it totals one hundred cubits from front to back. The western building with its separate yard and surrounding walls also measures one hundred cubits long. Across the eastern front, the courtyard and the temple facade together measure another hundred cubits wide.

The guide measures the western building facing the courtyard at the rear, including its upper balconies, and it is one hundred cubits. The prophet then turns his attention to the interior finish of the holy rooms and porticoes. Every part of the sacred structure was measured and laid out with deliberate precision.

The thresholds, narrow windows, and balconies were covered with fine wood paneling on every side. The wood covered the walls from the floor up to the windows, and the windows themselves were shielded with lattice-work. Definite measurements were given for the spaces above the doors and along every wall, inside and outside.

Carvings of cherubim and palm trees were placed alternately around all the inner walls of the house. Unlike the heavenly cherubim who each had four faces, these carved figures showed two faces on the flat surface: the face of a man looking toward a palm tree on one side, and the face of a young lion looking toward a palm tree on the other. These designs showed intelligence and strength united under God's rule.

The decorative carvings of cherubim and palm trees extended from the floor up to the space above the entrance doors. This artwork lined the entire main wall of the Holy Place. God's house was filled with beauty that reminded worshipers of the heavenly host and fruitful life.

The doorposts of the Holy Place were squared rather than rounded like columns. The entrance into the Most Holy Place was crafted in the very same square style. This harmony in design linked the outer room and the inner sanctuary into one balanced whole.

Inside the room stands a wooden altar that is three cubits high and two cubits square, with wooden corners, base, and sides. The guide explains that this is the table that stands before the Lord. It served as the altar of incense, where sweet smoke was offered before the Lord's presence, rather than for burning animal sacrifices.

differ.view: Calling the altar a table indicates that under the gospel, the bloody sacrifice is finished and believers now feast spiritually at the Lord's table.

notes.meaning: Both the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place had sets of double doors. Each door had two swinging panels that folded open on hinges. This allowed priests to pass through without having to open the entire wide entrance every time.

The doors of the sanctuary were carved with the same cherubim and palm trees found on the walls, and a wooden overhang or canopy covered the front porch outside. The side walls of the porch had narrow windows and carvings of palm trees, though without cherubim, marking them as outer areas. God directed every detail so that the closer one drew to His presence, the greater the holiness and dignity became.
